title: Privacy by Choosing Less
goals: Justify which information a stated task needs and remove unnecessary fields
Distinguish reducing personal data from hiding a name
Design a simple access, retention and deletion plan for a classroom activity
vocabulary: Information about an identifiable person, including combinations that can identify someone
The specific job information is collected or used to do
Using only the information needed for a stated purpose
A rule and mechanism deciding who can see or use information
How long information is kept before an agreed deletion or other approved action

worked_example.title: Removing a name is only one change

rows: Hides the name on this sheet
A separate key can reconnect the code
Small or unusual groups may still reveal a choice

blocks.text: A code is not a promise of anonymity. If a teacher keeps a key connecting P07 to a pupil, the coded record can still be linked to that pupil. Even without a key, a combination such as an exact birthday, a team and a photograph may identify someone. Ask whether a reader could connect the information to a person, not just whether the name column is blank.

Totals also need context. A report saying that the only member of a tiny club chose music reveals that member’s choice. Our whole-class topic totals reveal less detail than individual rows, but we should not describe every possible total as automatically anonymous. Share only what the audience needs for the purpose.

guided_practice.title: Challenge a claim of anonymity
guided_practice.prompt: A teacher replaces names with codes and keeps a separate code-to-name key. A pupil calls the records anonymous. Explain the problem. Then explain why removing names while leaving photographs would not settle the question either.
guided_practice.answer: The key can reconnect each code to a person, so the coded records are not anonymous just because names are absent. Restricting the key helps limit access but does not erase the link. Photographs can identify people even if the name field is removed.

independent_case.title: Design a different minimal-data task
independent_case.task: A fictional library wants only the total number of books needing repair in each category: cover, page or binding. It does not need to contact borrowers. A draft repair sheet asks for borrower name, home address, book repair category and borrower photograph. Design a plan: state the purpose, required and removed fields, who handles source sheets, what totals are shared with the librarian, and who disposes of sheets at what agreed point. Use no real borrower details.
independent_case.answer: Purpose: count repair needs by category. Keep repair category; remove borrower name, address and photograph because no borrower contact is required. An assigned teacher or librarian handles the source sheets, checks counts and shares category totals with the librarian. Name that adult as responsible for disposal after totals are verified and the counting task closes, following the agreed school process. Other justified restricted roles and clear disposal triggers are acceptable.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: More data always improves a task
Unnecessary identity fields do not improve a category count and create more information to manage.
Codes or missing names mean anonymous
A key or other identifying fields may reconnect records to a person.
Every total is safe to publish
A small or distinctive group may allow a reader to infer a person’s choice.
Deleting one copy proves all copies are gone
Other copies, screenshots or backups may remain; follow the adult-led school process.

Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.

blocks.text: INPUT  candidate information fields
PROCESS  keep only fields needed for the stated goal
OUTPUT  useful result with reduced privacy risk
CORE IDEA  A useful system should collect only information it truly needs.

UNDER THE HOOD  Data minimization limits collection, access, retention, and reuse to what is necessary for a defined purpose. Less data reduces breach exposure and misuse, but essential high-stakes information still needs secure, consent-aware handling.

A closer explanation

blocks.title: A small information plan for a fictional vote
blocks.caption: Purpose: choose a workshop topic. Collect the minimum, limit access, share the required result and agree how long the source slips are kept.

blocks.text: Suppose the fictional counts are drawing 8, music 7 and coding 5. These totals support the choice of drawing. There is no need to publish each slip or a photograph of a child holding it. The teacher checks the total of 20 against the number of slips and then follows the agreed school process for disposing of the slips after verification.

A retention plan needs a clear trigger and a responsible person: for example, the teacher disposes of the fictional vote slips after the totals are checked and the activity closes. Real classroom records must follow the school’s approved process. Deleting one visible copy does not prove that every backup, screenshot or previously shared copy is gone.

Comparison picture for Home address: not needed; remove

blocks.text: CASE 1 — Allergy  Clue: needed for safe lunch filter. Meaning: relevant sensitive data.
CASE 2 — Favorite foods  Clue: useful for preference. Meaning: optional relevant data.
CASE 3 — Home address  Clue: not needed. Meaning: remove.
CASE 4 — Face photo  Clue: not needed for menu choice. Meaning: remove.
BOUNDARY  Useful does not mean permitted forever or for every new purpose.
